description: Estudiantes de Ingeniería en Software y Tecnologías Emergentes
summary:
We developed Lunar Base, a game that trains children to be astronauts at a lunar base. Players must carefully consider which decisions to make, since a bad decision can threaten their stay on the Moon. To survive 14 Earth days, the length of one lunar day of sunlight, they complete hands-on mini-games that keep five vital bars (energy, oxygen, food, stress and sleep) in balance.

The game addresses the challenge by turning real NASA DONKI solar flare data into gameplay. Every three days a class C, M or X storm arrives, and each one demands a different response: taking refuge, cleaning dust from the solar panels, or calling Earth to shut down the greenhouse.

This matters because future lunar missions depend on astronauts who can make good decisions under pressure. By learning through play, children discover space weather and life-support challenges, and may be inspired to pursue careers in science and space exploration.
details: Lunar Base is a survival simulator in which you are the only astronaut on a lunar base and must survive 14 Earth days, the length of one lunar day of sunlight, by completing hands-on mini-games that keep five vital bars (energy, oxygen, food, stress and sleep) in balance. These bars drop over time as well as from your actions, so neglecting your tasks eventually kills you. Every three days a solar storm of class C, M or X arrives at a random time, built from real NASA DONKI flare data from May 2024 (class, duration, linked solar energetic particles, shield level and warning time). Each class demands a different response: you seal the shield doors to take refuge from a C flare, suit up and clean dust off the solar panels after an M flare, and call Earth to shut down the greenhouse during an X flare, which makes the food rot. Acting in time limits the damage, while failing or sleeping through the storm makes it far worse. The project teaches players about space weather and the real challenges of long-term life support, such as balancing oxygen, power, food and mental health. Its intended impact is to spark interest in heliophysics, space-weather forecasting and future lunar missions by letting players feel the pressure of a real flare warning. We built it in Python with the pygame library, used Git and GitHub for version control, and used the NASA DONKI API for the data. It runs on ordinary laptops with no special hardware, and the web build is made with pygbag. The project is creative because it turns real flare data into game mechanics, since the warning time sets the countdown and the shield level and particle radiation scale the consequences, and because every storm class needs a different mini-game response. Our team considered scientific accuracy, balance so the game is hard but fair, learning by doing instead of reading, accessibility with mouse-only controls and short mini-games, and keeping the scope achievable within the hackathon’s time limit.
